summary: Outlines a framework for using Robust Header Compression over IPsec security associations, compressing the inner headers to reduce overhead while keeping IPsec's protection. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret-envelope system adds a lot of extra writing, so this shows how to shorten the repeated parts inside.

subtitle: Compressing packet headers inside encrypted tunnels to reduce bandwidth overhead.

tldr.problem: IPsec tunnels add significant overhead (at least 50 bytes per packet in IPv6) that is especially wasteful in bandwidth-constrained networks. The benefits of encryption come at the cost of efficiency.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC (Robust Header Compression) is moved from hop-by-hop operation to the IPsec tunnel endpoints, where it compresses the inner headers before encryption, then decompresses them on the other end.
tldr.outcome: ROHCoIPsec reduces per-packet overhead while keeping IPsec's security properties intact. The trade-off is added complexity in IKE negotiation and potential challenges with packet reordering.

facts.label: SA modes supported
facts.value: Tunnel mode; transport mode compression of headers only

today: RFC 5856 is an Informational RFC and remains the framework for header compression over IPsec. Companion protocol specifications are RFC 5857 (IKEv2 extensions) and RFC 5858 (IPsec extensions).

sections.title: What ROHCoIPsec Solves
sections.content:
IPsec provides security for IP traffic but adds overhead when it tunnels packets between gateways. An Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) tunnel mode on an IPv6 flow adds at least 50 bytes of overhead per packet, which is wasteful on bandwidth-constrained links like wireless and satellite networks.

This document outlines a framework for integrating Robust Header Compression (ROHC) at IPsec Security Association endpoints. By compressing the transport layer headers (such as TCP and UDP) and the inner IP header before encryption, ROHCoIPsec reduces overhead while keeping IPsec's security guarantees.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of compressing mail headers as it travels from house to house, compress them once at the post office entrance and decompress at the exit. This saves space inside the encrypted envelope.

sections.title: How ROHCoIPsec Works
sections.content:
ROHC normally compresses packet headers on a hop-by-hop basis, where every router along the path can participate. ROHCoIPsec changes this: it applies compression between the two endpoints of an IPsec Security Association.

For outbound traffic, an IPsec device compresses the inner IP and transport headers using ROHC, then encrypts and authenticates the compressed packet. For inbound traffic, the device decrypts the packet, decompresses the inner headers, and processes them normally.

ROHC can operate in unidirectional mode (one-way compression on a single SA) or bidirectional mode (using a pair of SAs, one for data and one for feedback from the decompressor to the compressor). Feedback is necessary for ROHC to adapt to changing network conditions, but it must be sent sparingly because it itself traverses the IPsec tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender squeezes the letter, puts it in the secret envelope, and sends it. The receiver opens the envelope and unsqueezes the letter. If the receiver notices something wrong, they send a tiny note back asking the sender to re-send.

sections.title: The Integration Framework
sections.content:
The ROHCoIPsec framework requires changes to both ROHC and IPsec. The Security Association (SA) state must include a flag indicating whether ROHC is enabled for that SA. When ROHC is enabled, the Next Header field in the ESP or AH header uses the value 142, the IANA-assigned protocol identifier for ROHC.

Three paths are possible: if the packet is compressed, the Next Header field signals ROHC and the inner headers are compressed (Path 1). If the packet arrives at the compressor but cannot be compressed, the Next Header field indicates the original protocol and the packet is sent uncompressed (Path 2). If ROHC is disabled for the SA, the packet follows normal IPsec processing without any compression attempt (Path 3).

Channel parameter configuration for ROHC is handled by IKEv2, the Internet Key Exchange protocol, rather than by link-layer negotiation as in hop-by-hop ROHC.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail system checks a flag: Is compression enabled? If yes, it tries to squeeze the letter. If it can't squeeze it or compression is off, it sends it normally. A special code tells the receiver whether the letter was squeezed.

sections.title: Integrity and Reordering Challenges
sections.content:
ROHC is designed to handle packet loss and reordering. However, under significant packet loss or adversarial reordering, erroneous packets may be constructed at the decompressor and forwarded into the protected domain, even though the RFC notes that ROHC's integrity mechanisms work best for random packet loss, not malicious attacks.

To address this, ROHCoIPsec can apply an additional integrity check (ICV) to the original packet before compression. This ICV ensures that if a decompressed packet does not match the original, it will be dropped.

Implementations should consider using ROHC version 2 profiles, which include mechanisms for robustness over reordering channels. IPsec's sequence number can also help the decompressor identify late or reordered packets.

A malicious or malfunctioning compressor could send erroneous packets to the decompressor, or a malicious decompressor could discard valid packets or refuse to decompress, both causing denial of service. Strong integrity-check algorithms mitigate these risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes squeezed letters get jumbled in the envelope. A special check number inside confirms the letter is good. If something is wrong, the receiver throws it away instead of reading garbage.

sections.title: Path MTU and Future Work
sections.content:
IPsec already increases packet size through tunneling and authentication tags. ROHC compression can sometimes increase size (when compression is ineffective) and the additional integrity check value (ICV) adds more bytes. All of this can trigger Path MTU Discovery issues, where packets are too large to transmit on some network links.

The specification outlines approaches in detail for handling these MTU challenges, including fragmenting before or after IPsec processing, or discarding packets when the Don't Fragment bit is set.

ROHCoIPsec is described as straightforward to specify because IPsec SA endpoints provide clear source-destination pairs for compression and decompression. However, full protocol specifications for IKEv2 extensions and IPsec processing are defined in companion documents (RFC 5857 and RFC 5858).
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes squeezing makes things bigger instead of smaller. If the package gets too big for the mail truck, special rules decide what to do: cut it up or send it back.
